paragraphs.heading: The atom's core
paragraphs.text: The atomic nucleus is the small, dense center of an atom, made of protons and neutrons. Around it lies a cloud of negatively charged electrons, held to the positive nucleus by electrostatic force. Nearly all of an atom's mass is in the nucleus, with the electrons adding very little. The nuclear force is what binds the protons and neutrons together.

paragraphs.heading: How small it is
paragraphs.text: Nuclear sizes are given in femtometers (fm), where 1.70 fm is 1.70×10⁻¹⁵ m. A hydrogen nucleus, which is a single proton, is about 1.70 fm across, and a uranium nucleus about 11.7 fm. The whole atom, nucleus plus electron cloud, is far bigger: about 27,000 times wider than its nucleus for uranium and about 60,000 times for hydrogen.

paragraphs.heading: Testing the plum pudding
paragraphs.text: The nucleus was found in 1911, when Ernest Rutherford set out to test the atom model Thomson had proposed, known as the plum pudding model. In that model, an atom was negative electrons scattered at random through a sphere of positive charge. With Hans Geiger and the help of Ernest Marsden, Rutherford aimed alpha particles, which are helium nuclei, at a thin sheet of metal foil. If Thomson was right, the positive alpha particles should have passed through with barely any change of course. Instead, many were knocked aside at very large angles.

paragraphs.heading: What the experiment showed
paragraphs.text: An alpha particle has about 7,000 times the mass of an electron, so turning it aside needed a very strong force. Rutherford saw that the plum pudding model could not be accurate. The deflections made sense only if positive and negative charge were kept apart and the atom's mass was packed into a point of positive charge. That backed the picture of a nuclear atom with a dense center of charge and mass. Rutherford made the discovery at the University of Manchester, building on the 1909 Geiger–Marsden gold foil experiment.

paragraphs.heading: Protons and neutrons
paragraphs.text: Protons and neutrons are themselves made of more elementary particles called quarks. Protons carry all of a nucleus's charge, and so set its chemical identity. Neutrons have no charge, but they add nearly as much mass as protons do. Neutrons explain isotopes, atoms with the same atomic number but different atomic mass, and their main role is to reduce the electric repulsion inside the nucleus.

paragraphs.heading: What holds it together
paragraphs.text: The nucleus is held together by the residual strong force, also called the nuclear force. It is a small leftover of the strong interaction, which binds quarks into protons and neutrons. At the usual spacing between protons and neutrons it pulls very hard, overpowering the electric repulsion between protons, and that is what lets nuclei exist. Its range is very short, and it drops to almost nothing just past the edge of the nucleus.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The word comes from the Latin nucleus, a small form of nux, meaning nut, used for the kernel inside a watery fruit such as a peach. Michael Faraday used it in 1844 for the central point of an atom. Rutherford proposed its modern atomic meaning in 1912.
